title: Sitting down on the shore
hook: late, empty-handed, and tempted to hide or give up

segments.voice: Yesterday: Svayamprabha led them out with eyes covered, a sattvic gift that asked nothing back. But the month was already gone.

On the beach, Angada does the math, and it's bad. They're late. They haven't found Sita. Sugriva warned that anyone who came back late would answer with their life. And Angada carries a private fear on top of that. He's Vali's son. His uncle took his father's throne with Rama's help. Angada wonders whether Sugriva has ever really trusted him. Back late and empty-handed? He decides he isn't going back at all.
screen: `ANGADA DOES THE MATH.` → `A PRIVATE FEAR.` → `HE WON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Despair spreads fast. Angada tells the others he'll fast to death right here on the shore, a vow called prayopavesha. One monkey, named Tara, a different Tara from Vali's widow, offers another way out: let's go back to the cave. It has food, water, safety, and no one could reach us. Several monkeys like the idea. Then Hanuman speaks. To Angada he's gentle: Sugriva is fair, and you're dear to him; don't assume the worst. About the cave he's blunt: Lakshmana's arrows could split that cave open. Hiding isn't safety. And quietly he wins the others over, one by one. Angada isn't convinced. He spreads sacred darbha grass on the shore and sits down, and the others sit with him, a long line along the sea, talking about Rama and Sita, and about Jatayu, the old vulture who died fighting Ravana. Hindus know this posture. The Bhagavad Gita opens with it: the warrior Arjuna, facing a duty he can't bear, drops his bow and sinks down in his chariot. Krishna's first answer, more or less, is: stand up. The teaching under both scenes is dharma, your rightful duty, the part that's yours to do. Being late doesn't cancel it. Being afraid doesn't cancel it. Despair says sit down and disappear; dharma says go back, tell the truth, and keep going. And up on the hillside behind them, out of a cave, something very old is listening.
screen: `PRAYOPAVESHA: A FAST TO DEATH.` · `HANUMAN: HIDING ISN'T SAFETY.` · `ARJUNA SAT DOWN TOO.` · `DESPAIR DOESN'T CANCEL YOUR DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Notice, gently, whether there's somewhere in your life you've quietly sat down and given up, not to fix it now, just to see it. Breathe in and name it; breathe out and ask what your part there still is, one small next step: a call, an apology, showing up late instead of never. If you pray, many Hindus call on Hanuman when they're afraid; you can too. If giving up ever feels like more than that, please reach out today: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Prayopavesha, sitting down to fast unto death: the vow Angada takes today on the shore, when Hanuman argues that hiding in the cave isn't safety either.
Your line: despair doesn't cancel your dharma. Even here, the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Prayopavesha, fasting unto death, appears in the epics as a solemn vow; Hindu teachers today speak of it only in very specific traditional contexts, and in the Ramayana the monkeys' vow is interrupted before it's carried out.

prayopavesha.meaning: a vow to sit and fast unto death

darbha.meaning: a sacred grass used in rites

dharma.meaning: rightful duty; the part that's yours to do
